claim: The β-globin reporter gene construct contains 24X PP7 RNA hairpins in the second intron and 24X MS2 hairpin cassette in the 3′ UTR.
source: We stably integrated into U2-OS cells, a human β-globin reporter with a DNA cassette that encodes for 24X PP7 RNA hairpins in the second intron (Chao et al., 2008) and a 24X MS2 hairpin cassette in the 3′ UTR (Boireau et al., 2007) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript directly describes the reporter construct design with specific details about the number and location of RNA hairpins.

claim: PCP-mCherry and MCP-GFP bind to RNA stem loops with high affinity, with MCP having an on rate of 0.54 μM–1s–1.
source: The constitutively expressed PP7-coat protein tagged with mCherry (PCP-mCherry) and MS2-coat protein tagged with GFP (MCP-GFP) bind with high affinity (the on rate for MCP is 0.54 μM–1s–1. At a nuclear concentration of 1 μM, the average time for the MCP to bind a completed stem loop is 1.85 s) (Buenrostro et al., 2014) to the RNA stem loops as homodimers, tagging each cassette with 48 fluorophores of a single color, resulting in orthogonal labeling of two different parts of the nascent transcript (Hocine et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2013; Buenrostro et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a specific kinetic parameter for MCP binding from a published study.

claim: At a nuclear concentration of 1 μM, the average time for MCP to bind a completed stem loop is 1.85 s.
source: The constitutively expressed PP7-coat protein tagged with mCherry (PCP-mCherry) and MS2-coat protein tagged with GFP (MCP-GFP) bind with high affinity (the on rate for MCP is 0.54 μM–1s–1. At a nuclear concentration of 1 μM, the average time for the MCP to bind a completed stem loop is 1.85 s) (Buenrostro et al., 2014) to the RNA stem loops as homodimers, tagging each cassette with 48 fluorophores of a single color, resulting in orthogonal labeling of two different parts of the nascent transcript (Hocine et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2013; Buenrostro et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript provides a calculated binding time based on the on rate and nuclear concentration, citing a published study.

claim: Each cassette is tagged with 48 fluorophores of a single color.
source: The constitutively expressed PP7-coat protein tagged with mCherry (PCP-mCherry) and MS2-coat protein tagged with GFP (MCP-GFP) bind with high affinity (the on rate for MCP is 0.54 μM–1s–1. At a nuclear concentration of 1 μM, the average time for the MCP to bind a completed stem loop is 1.85 s) (Buenrostro et al., 2014) to the RNA stem loops as homodimers, tagging each cassette with 48 fluorophores of a single color, resulting in orthogonal labeling of two different parts of the nascent transcript (Hocine et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2013; Buenrostro et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript states that homodimers bind to 24 stem loops, resulting in 48 fluorophores per cassette.

claim: Unspliced RNAs appear in both colors (red and green), while spliced RNAs are only visible in green.
source: Since the PP7 cassette is intronic, unspliced RNAs appear in both colors, while spliced RNAs are only visible in green.
evidence: The manuscript explains the logic of the dual-color labeling system based on the location of the PP7 cassette in the intron.

claim: Time-lapse imaging reveals a temporally fluctuating diffraction-limited spot co-localizing in both colors that corresponds to the transcription site.
source: Time-lapse imaging of cells in 3D reveals a temporally fluctuating diffraction-limited spot, co-localizing in both colors, that corresponds to the transcription site (TS) where nascent transcripts are synthesized (Figure 1B–C, Videos 1 and Videos 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from time-lapse imaging and references figures and videos showing the transcription site.

claim: Mature mRNA (exon only) diffuses in both the nucleus and the cytoplasm.
source: We observed mature mRNA (exon only) diffusing in both the nucleus and the cytoplasm (Video 3), and we verified expression of the protein product, indicating the message is spliced and translated correctly (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The manuscript reports direct observations of mRNA localization from imaging data.

claim: The reporter gene is spliced and translated correctly as verified by protein product expression.
source: We observed mature mRNA (exon only) diffusing in both the nucleus and the cytoplasm (Video 3), and we verified expression of the protein product, indicating the message is spliced and translated correctly (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The manuscript states that protein product expression was verified, indicating correct splicing and translation.

claim: Both pre- and post-release splicing are visible as single events at the same gene over time.
source: We find that both pre- and post-release splicing are visible as single events at the same gene over time (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of both types of splicing events from time-lapse imaging data.

claim: In post-release splicing, the intronic fluorescence appears, followed by the exon fluorescence, followed by a coincidental drop in both colors reflecting the release of an unspliced RNA.
source: In the case of post-release splicing, the intronic fluorescence appears, followed by the exon fluorescence, followed by a coincidental drop in both colors reflecting the release of an unspliced RNA (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal sequence of fluorescence signals characteristic of post-release splicing.

claim: For pre-release splicing, there is a delay between the drop-off of the red and green signals, indicating intron removal before release.
source: For pre-release splicing, there is a delay between the drop-off of the red and green signals, indicating intron removal before release (Figure 1E).
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal sequence of fluorescence signals characteristic of pre-release splicing.

claim: Diffusion of the pre-mRNA away from the transcription site is rapid, accounting for the precipitous drop of the signal in the time trace.
source: Diffusion of the pre-mRNA away from the TS is rapid, which accounts for the precipitous drop of the signal in the time trace (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript explains the observed signal drop as a consequence of rapid diffusion.

claim: The correlation functions for β-globin reveal kinetic features hidden in the fluorescence time traces and encapsulate the stochastic kinetics of single-transcript synthesis.
source: The correlation functions for β-globin (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B) reveal the kinetic features hidden in the fluorescence time traces and encapsulate the stochastic kinetics of single-transcript synthesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1—§2).
evidence: The manuscript states that correlation analysis reveals kinetic information from the time traces.

claim: At short time delays (<40 s), the cross-correlation reflects the order of splicing and release events.
source: At short time delays (<40 s), the cross-correlation reflects the order of splicing and release events (Figure 2B–C and Supplementary file 1—§2).
evidence: The manuscript explains how short-delay cross-correlation features relate to the temporal order of molecular events.

claim: Splicing occurs before release for 13 ± 5% of β-globin transcripts.
source: The experimental cross-correlation determined from ∼2000 individual β-globin transcripts indicates that splicing occurs before release for a fraction of transcripts (13 ± 5%, Figure 2B inset).
evidence: The manuscript reports a quantitative measurement of pre-release splicing fraction from correlation analysis.

claim: Splicing and release are not firmly constrained to occur in a specific order (p < 0.003).
source: In summary, these data demonstrate that splicing and release are not firmly constrained to occur in a specific order (p < 0.003).
evidence: The manuscript provides a statistical conclusion about the stochastic nature of splicing and release order.

claim: The delay at which the intron-to-exon cross-correlation starts decreasing (∼60 s) corresponds to the elongation time between the two cassettes (2573 bases apart), resulting in an elongation rate of ∼2.6 kb/min.
source: For example, the delay at which the intron-to-exon cross-correlation (Figure 2B, blue circles) starts decreasing (∼60 s) corresponds to the elongation time between the two cassettes (2573 bases apart), resulting in an elongation rate of ∼2.6 kb/min.
evidence: The manuscript calculates elongation rate from the cross-correlation decay time and known distance between cassettes.

claim: The decay at time-scales > 100 s relates to the dwell time of transcripts at the transcription site.
source: Finally, the decay at time-scales > 100 s relates to the dwell time of transcripts at the TS (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The manuscript interprets long-timescale correlation decay as reflecting transcript dwell time.

claim: RNA is not immediately released after transcription of the poly(A) site but remains at the transcription site for a duration reflecting either a pause at/near the poly(A) site, transcription past the termination site, or post-cleavage retention.
source: Specifically, the long decays observed in all correlation functions indicates that RNA is not immediately released after transcription of the poly(A) site. Rather, the transcript remains at the TS for a duration which reflects either a pause at/near the poly(A) site, transcription past the termination site, or a post-cleavage retention of the transcript within the diffraction-limited spot (Hofer and Darnell, 1981; Glover-Cutter et al., 2008; Brody et al., 2011; Carrillo Oesterreich et al., 2010; Bhatt et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript interprets correlation function decay as evidence for transcript retention and cites supporting literature.

claim: Treatment with camptothecin (CPT) resulted in a marked shift of the decreasing part of the intron-to-exon cross-correlation to longer delays, which is the expected manifestation of slower elongation.
source: Treatment with camptothecin (CPT, a topoisomerase I inhibitor known to slow down elongation [Singh and Padgett, 2009]) resulted in a marked shift of the decreasing part of the intron-to-exon cross-correlation to longer delays (Figure 2E), which is the expected manifestation of slower elongation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B, Supplementary file 1—§2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the effect of CPT treatment on correlation functions and cites literature on CPT's mechanism.

claim: When shuffling channels between traces or using time traces recorded away from the transcription site, the correlation functions are flat, supporting that the correlation functions reflect molecular events at the transcription site.
source: As an additional control, when shuffling channels between traces or when using time traces recorded away from the TS, the correlation functions are flat (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–H), supporting the fact that the correlation functions shown on Figure 2B reflect the molecular events happening at the TS.
evidence: The manuscript describes control experiments that validate the correlation analysis method.

claim: Correlation functions reveal single-transcript kinetics even from signals where multiple transcripts are present at any given time.
source: Finally, we emphasize that an essential advantage of this approach is that correlation functions reveal single-transcript kinetics even from signals where multiple transcripts are present at any given time (Supplementary file 1—§1).
evidence: The manuscript explains a key advantage of the correlation analysis approach.

claim: After averaging over many transcription and splicing events, inter-transcript correlations disappear, leaving only a central peak which reflects the kinetics of single transcripts.
source: After averaging over many transcription and splicing events, inter-transcript correlations disappear, leaving only a central peak which reflects the kinetics of single transcripts (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript explains how averaging eliminates inter-transcript correlations to reveal single-transcript kinetics.

claim: The best model for β-globin transcription and splicing is one from scheme II, where splicing is independent of elongation and transcript release.
source: The three other schemes were better at fitting the correlation curves but the best model is one from scheme II, that is where splicing is independent of elongation and transcript release (See Figure 2—figure supplement 5 and discussion on Model comparison in 'Materials and methods').
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of model comparison analysis.

claim: In the best-fit model, splicing occurs a fixed amount of time after the 3′ splice site has been transcribed, and transcript release involves a stochastic delay after the poly(A) site is reached.
source: In this 3-parameter model (Table 1), splicing occurs a fixed amount of time after the 3′ss has been transcribed, and transcript release involves a stochastic delay after the poly(A) site is reached.
evidence: The manuscript describes the characteristics of the best-fit model.

claim: The β-globin-terminal intron splicing time was 267 ± 9 s after the polymerase passes the 3′ splice site.
source: In total, the β-globin-terminal intron splicing time was 267 ± 9 s after the polymerase passes the 3′ ss.
evidence: The manuscript reports a quantitative measurement from model fitting.

claim: The measured splicing time is consistent with previous estimates either in vivo on cell populations or in vitro at the single-molecule level.
source: This measurement of splicing time is consistent with previous estimates either in vivo on cell populations (Singh and Padgett, 2009) or in vitro at the single-molecule level (Hoskins et al., 2011), suggesting that PP7 stem loops do not perturb splicing kinetics of this intron, contrary to MS2 stem loops (Aitken et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript compares their measurement to published values and cites relevant literature.

claim: PP7 stem loops do not perturb splicing kinetics of this intron, contrary to MS2 stem loops.
source: This measurement of splicing time is consistent with previous estimates either in vivo on cell populations (Singh and Padgett, 2009) or in vitro at the single-molecule level (Hoskins et al., 2011), suggesting that PP7 stem loops do not perturb splicing kinetics of this intron, contrary to MS2 stem loops (Aitken et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript infers that PP7 loops do not perturb splicing based on consistency with previous measurements and cites literature on MS2 effects.

claim: The average red-to-green ratio of 1.41 is indistinguishable from the expected 1.4 value predicted by modeling analysis.
source: As an independent validation of our modeling results, we counted the number of red and green RNAs at transcription sites using a normalized ratiometric approach (Zenklusen et al., 2008) (See 'Materials and methods' and Figure 2—figure supplement 6). The average red-to-green ratio of 1.41 is indistinguishable from the expected 1.4 value predicted by our modeling analysis of the correlation functions.
evidence: The manuscript reports an independent validation measurement that agrees with model predictions.

claim: Both SSA and CPT drug treatments only affected a single parameter, arguing that splicing is kinetically independent of elongation/termination.
source: Importantly, both SSA and CPT drug treatments only affected a single parameter (Table 1), arguing that splicing is kinetically independent of elongation/termination.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the selective effects of drug treatments as evidence for kinetic independence.

claim: Splicing occurring at the transcription site is rarely completed during elongation but rather during a pause at the 3′ end of the gene.
source: Based on our measurements, splicing occurring at the TS is rarely completed during elongation but rather during a pause at the 3′ end of the gene.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from their kinetic measurements.

claim: Because transcript release is stochastic, the 3′ end dwell time can be shorter or longer than the necessary time to remove the intron, resulting in splicing that can occur either before or after release.
source: Because transcript release is stochastic, the 3′ end dwell time can be shorter or longer than the necessary time to remove the intron, resulting in splicing that can occur either before or after release.
evidence: The manuscript explains how stochastic dwell time leads to variable splicing outcomes.

claim: A mobile population of unspliced pre-mRNA (co-localized intron/exon) was observed diffusing in the immediate vicinity of the transcription site.
source: We observed a mobile population of unspliced pre-mRNA (co-localized intron/exon) diffusing in the immediate vicinity of the TS (Figure 4A–B, Video 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports direct observations from confocal imaging.

claim: Spliced mRNA (exon only) could be observed diffusing throughout the nucleus.
source: In contrast, spliced mRNA (exon only) could be observed diffusing throughout the nucleus.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of spliced mRNA distribution.

claim: The radial distribution of mRNA and pre-mRNA indicated an enrichment for unspliced transcripts within 2.4 ± 0.1 µm of the transcription site.
source: The radial distribution of mRNA and pre-mRNA indicated an enrichment for unspliced transcripts within 2.4 ± 0.1 µm of the TS (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), meaning that splicing occurs faster than diffusion throughout the nucleus.
evidence: The manuscript reports a quantitative measurement of spatial distribution and its interpretation.

claim: Splicing occurs faster than diffusion throughout the nucleus.
source: The radial distribution of mRNA and pre-mRNA indicated an enrichment for unspliced transcripts within 2.4 ± 0.1 µm of the TS (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), meaning that splicing occurs faster than diffusion throughout the nucleus.
evidence: The manuscript infers the relative rates of splicing and diffusion from spatial distribution data.

claim: Upon treatment with splicing inhibitor SSA, the enrichment for unspliced transcripts near the transcription site disappears, with most transcripts unspliced and dispersed throughout the nucleus.
source: This enrichment disappears upon treatment with splicing inhibitor SSA, in which case most of the transcripts are unspliced and dispersed throughout the nucleus (Figure 4C, Video 6).
evidence: The manuscript reports the effect of SSA treatment on spatial distribution.

claim: The diffusion coefficient of mRNA in the nucleus is D = 0.12 µm2/s.
source: From the measured diffusion coefficient (D = 0.12 µm2/s, Figure 4—figure supplement 2; See 'Materials and methods'), we calculated that post-release splicing takes place on average 13 ± 1 s after departure from chromatin.
evidence: The manuscript reports a measured diffusion coefficient from RICS analysis.

claim: Post-release splicing takes place on average 13 ± 1 s after departure from chromatin.
source: From the measured diffusion coefficient (D = 0.12 µm2/s, Figure 4—figure supplement 2; See 'Materials and methods'), we calculated that post-release splicing takes place on average 13 ± 1 s after departure from chromatin.
evidence: The manuscript reports a calculated splicing time based on diffusion coefficient and spatial distribution.

claim: Post-release splicing time (13 s) is much shorter than the expected 137 s if pre- and post-release splicing kinetics were identical.
source: This time is much shorter than the expected 137 s it would take if pre- and post-release splicing kinetics were identical (calculated from Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript compares the measured post-release splicing time to a calculated expectation.

claim: 3′ end retention time is not affected by SSA treatment.
source: However, this interpretation is inconsistent with the fact that 3′end retention time is not affected by SSA treatment which impairs binding of U2 and hence affects recruitment of all the snRNPs except U1 (Corrionero et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript reports an observation from SSA treatment experiments and cites literature on SSA's mechanism.

claim: Introns can be retained for over 4 min on chromatin.
source: In summary, although introns can be retained for over 4 min on chromatin, once the transcript is released, splicing is 10-fold faster for freely diffusing transcripts.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the timescale of intron retention on chromatin.

claim: Once the transcript is released, splicing is 10-fold faster for freely diffusing transcripts than on chromatin.
source: In summary, although introns can be retained for over 4 min on chromatin, once the transcript is released, splicing is 10-fold faster for freely diffusing transcripts.
evidence: The manuscript compares splicing rates on chromatin versus after release.

claim: In most cases, the nascent intron is retained until transcription reaches the 3′ end of the gene and then removed either before or shortly after release of the transcript.
source: In most cases, the nascent intron is retained until transcription reaches the 3′ end of the gene and then removed either before or shortly after release of the transcript (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the typical pathway for intron removal.

claim: The serine-to-phenylalanine (S34F) missense mutation in the zinc finger domain of U2AF1 results in disparate changes in alternative splicing patterns including exon skipping, exon inclusion, and alternative 3′ splice site selection.
source: The serine-to-phenylalanine (S34F) missense mutation in the zinc finger domain results in disparate changes in alternative splicing patterns including exon skipping, exon inclusion, and alternative 3′ ss selection (Brooks et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites published findings on the effects of the U2AF1-S34F mutation.

claim: U2AF1-S34F completely abolishes pre-release splicing.
source: Correlation functions revealed that U2AF1-S34F completely abolishes pre-release splicing (Figure 6A, horizontal slope) and prolongs transcript 3′ end dwell time (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the effect of U2AF1-S34F on splicing timing from correlation analysis.

claim: U2AF1-S34F prolongs transcript 3′ end dwell time.
source: Correlation functions revealed that U2AF1-S34F completely abolishes pre-release splicing (Figure 6A, horizontal slope) and prolongs transcript 3′ end dwell time (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the effect of U2AF1-S34F on dwell time from model fitting.

claim: In the presence of U2AF1-S34F, all transcripts are post-transcriptionally spliced at a slower rate (27 ± 3 s).
source: Post-release imaging of transcripts showed a local enrichment for unspliced pre-mRNA near the TS, but with a greater spatial extent in the case of U2AF1-S34F (Figure 6B–C, Video 7). Thus, all transcripts are post-transcriptionally spliced, albeit at a slower rate (27 ± 3 s; Figure 6D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the effect of U2AF1-S34F on post-release splicing rate from spatial distribution analysis.

claim: U2AF1-S34F does not affect splicing efficiency, poly(A) length, or 3′ UTR length.
source: Splicing efficiency, poly(A) length, and 3′ UTR length were unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The manuscript reports measurements showing no effect of U2AF1-S34F on these parameters.

claim: The mutant U2AF1-S34F delays splicing to post-release, slows splicing from freely diffusing transcripts, but has no detectable effect on splicing efficiency.
source: In summary, these data suggest that the mutant delays splicing to post-release, slows splicing from freely diffusing transcripts, but has no detectable effect on splicing efficiency.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the effects of U2AF1-S34F mutation.

claim: Expression of U2AF1-S34F resulted in an increase in the level of unspliced FXR1 pre-mRNA in the nucleus (16.0 ± 0.4% compared to 6.0 ± 0.3%).
source: Expression of the U2AF1-S34F mutant resulted both in an increase in the level of unspliced pre-mRNA in the nucleus (16.0 ± 0.4% compared to 6.0 ± 0.3%, Figure 6F) and the radial distance from the TS (1.8 ± 0.5 μm compared to 0.5 ± 0.2 μm, Figure 6G).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements of unspliced FXR1 pre-mRNA levels from FISH experiments.

claim: Expression of U2AF1-S34F resulted in an increase in the radial distance of unspliced FXR1 pre-mRNA from the transcription site (1.8 ± 0.5 μm compared to 0.5 ± 0.2 μm).
source: Expression of the U2AF1-S34F mutant resulted both in an increase in the level of unspliced pre-mRNA in the nucleus (16.0 ± 0.4% compared to 6.0 ± 0.3%, Figure 6F) and the radial distance from the TS (1.8 ± 0.5 μm compared to 0.5 ± 0.2 μm, Figure 6G).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements of spatial distribution from FISH experiments.

claim: The S34F mutation in U2AF1 acts in a dominant negative fashion to postpone splicing until after release and cause slower splicing from diffusing transcripts.
source: Taken together, both static and dynamic measurements on a reporter β-globin transcript and the endogenous FXR1 transcript suggest that the S34F mutation in U2AF1 acts in a dominant negative fashion to postpone splicing until after release and cause slower splicing from diffusing transcripts.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion about the mechanism of U2AF1-S34F based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The β-globin-terminal intron can be spliced during multiple steps of the transcription cycle.
source: The picture that emerges from this study is one in which the β-globin-terminal intron can be spliced during multiple steps of the transcription cycle (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: A minority of transcripts are spliced while retained at the 3′ end of the gene, but the dominant pathway is one in which splicing is contemporaneous with release or occurs shortly thereafter.
source: A minority of transcripts are spliced while retained at the 3′ end of the gene, but the dominant pathway is the one in which splicing is contemporaneous with release or occurs shortly thereafter.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the relative frequencies of different splicing pathways.

claim: Splicing is 10-fold faster on freely diffusing transcripts than on chromatin-bound transcripts.
source: In fact, we find that splicing is 10-fold faster on freely diffusing transcripts than on chromatin-bound transcripts.
evidence: The manuscript compares splicing rates in different contexts.

claim: Commitment to splicing of the terminal β-globin intron occurs co-transcriptionally.
source: Our data are consistent with a model where commitment to splicing of the terminal β-globin intron occurs co-transcriptionally but suggest there may be a high energy barrier to completion of intron removal while transcripts are still tethered to chromatin, possibly due to steric constraints.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a model based on their data.

claim: There may be a high energy barrier to completion of intron removal while transcripts are still tethered to chromatin, possibly due to steric constraints.
source: Our data are consistent with a model where commitment to splicing of the terminal β-globin intron occurs co-transcriptionally but suggest there may be a high energy barrier to completion of intron removal while transcripts are still tethered to chromatin, possibly due to steric constraints.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about a possible mechanism for slower chromatin-bound splicing.

claim: Post-release splicing may be the energetically favored process, but there is a long kinetic window in which the less-favorable pre-release intron removal can occur.
source: Thus, post-release splicing may be the energetically favored process, but there is a long kinetic window in which the less-favorable pre-release intron removal can occur.
evidence: The manuscript proposes an interpretation of the kinetic competition model.

claim: Population-based measurements suggest a splicing time for several endogenous, un-modified introns of 5–10 min.
source: Population-based measurements suggest a splicing time for several endogenous, un-modified introns of 5–10 min (Singh and Padgett, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites published measurements of splicing time.

claim: Bulk in vitro measurements on β-globin indicate a 40- to 50-min splicing timescale.
source: Bulk in vitro measurements on β-globin indicate a 40- to 50-min timescale.
evidence: The manuscript cites published in vitro measurements.

claim: A single-molecule in vitro study on yeast transcripts measured ∼10-min splicing time.
source: A single-molecule in vitro study on yeast transcripts measured ∼10-min splicing time.
evidence: The manuscript cites published single-molecule measurements.

claim: Previous live-cell imaging approaches indicate splicing times in the order of ∼30 s.
source: On the opposite end of the spectrum, previous live-cell imaging approaches relying on both direct and indirect measurements indicate splicing times in the order of ∼30 s (Huranová et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites published live-cell imaging measurements.

claim: The ability to observe the transcription and splicing process with a time resolution spanning three orders of magnitude is a primary experimental advance of this study.
source: One of the primary experimental advances in our study is the ability to observe the transcription and splicing process with a time resolution that spans three orders of magnitude.
evidence: The manuscript highlights a key methodological advantage of their approach.

claim: The time to splice is a distributed quantity, and splicing times vary from transcript to transcript.
source: Since the time to splice is a distributed quantity, and splicing times vary from transcript to transcript, the variation in previously reported splicing rates may be strongly influenced by the temporal dynamic range of the method.
evidence: The manuscript explains why different methods may report different splicing times.

claim: The splicing efficiency of the reporter is high (>95%).
source: Second, the splicing efficiency of the reporter is high (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), suggesting there are no dead-end intermediates.
evidence: The manuscript reports a measurement of splicing efficiency.

claim: Endogenous metazoan RNAs are decorated with RNA-binding proteins from their inception.
source: Third, endogenous metazoan RNAs are decorated with RNA-binding proteins from their inception (Castello et al., 2012), suggesting that the spliceosome is well-equipped to handle bulky messages.
evidence: The manuscript cites published findings about RNA-binding proteins on nascent RNA.

claim: The single-molecule study reveals the existence of multiple pathways, indicating the absence of a strict checkpoint for intron removal.
source: Importantly, our single-molecule study reveals the existence of multiple pathways, indicating the absence of a strict checkpoint for intron removal (Bird et al., 2005; Alexander et al., 2010; Brody et al., 2011; Carrillo Oesterreich et al., 2010; Bhatt et al., 2012; Pandya-Jones et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript states a key finding and cites related literature.

claim: None of the models which assume dependence between splicing and elongation/release fit better than one that assumes independence.
source: First, none of the models which assume dependence between splicing and elongation/release fit better than one that assumes independence.
evidence: The manuscript reports a result from model comparison analysis.

claim: Abolishing splicing with SSA does not lead to an increase in release times.
source: Abolishing splicing with SSA does not lead to an increase in release times.
evidence: The manuscript reports an observation from SSA treatment experiments.

claim: Splicing and release can happen in either order, with the order of events determined by kinetic competition.
source: Thus, splicing and release can happen in either order, with the order of events determined by kinetic competition.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the kinetic competition model.

claim: It is kinetic competition which results in stochastic outcomes for the RNA.
source: It is this competition which results in stochastic outcomes for the RNA.
evidence: The manuscript explains how kinetic competition leads to stochasticity.

claim: Single-cell variation in alternative splicing has been observed.
source: While, single-cell variation in alternative splicing has been observed, the mechanism behind this variability has remained elusive (Waks et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites published observations of single-cell splicing variability.

claim: Single-molecule measurements on fixed cells suggest that post-release splicing may be the preferred pathway for alternatively spliced transcripts.
source: Interestingly, single-molecule measurements on fixed cells suggest that post-release splicing may be the preferred pathway for alternatively spliced transcripts (Vargas et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites published findings on alternative splicing pathways.

claim: Studies on the mutant U2AF1 provide a mechanistic basis for the observation that post-release splicing may be preferred for alternatively spliced transcripts.
source: Our studies on the mutant U2AF1 provide a mechanistic basis for this observation and suggest a role for mutations in the core splicing machinery for the increased levels of 'noisy splicing' which are observed in cancer (Pickrell et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript connects their findings to published observations about splicing in cancer.

claim: Post-release splicing is more efficient than pre-release splicing.
source: Furthermore, our time-resolved results indicate that post-release splicing is more efficient than pre-release splicing, which may explain how the timing of intron removal might lead to different outcomes for the message.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from their kinetic measurements.

claim: The kinetic delay induced by U2AF1-S34F allows either for alternate pairing between 5′ and 3′ splice sites during transcription or for post-release reconfiguration of pre-mRNA which is not yet committed to intron excision in the spliceosome.
source: We speculate that the kinetic delay induced by U2AF1-S34F allows either for alternate pairing between 5′ and 3′ss during transcription or for post-release reconfiguration of pre-mRNA which is not yet committed to intron excision in the spliceosome.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about possible mechanisms for U2AF1-S34F effects.

claim: Kinetic competition governs the stochastic balance between multiple competing pathways for RNA synthesis and processing.
source: Our results show that kinetic competition governs the stochastic balance between multiple competing pathways for RNA synthesis and processing and that this balance is perturbed by oncogenic mutations.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The balance between competing pathways for RNA synthesis and processing is perturbed by oncogenic mutations.
source: Our results show that kinetic competition governs the stochastic balance between multiple competing pathways for RNA synthesis and processing and that this balance is perturbed by oncogenic mutations.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes a key finding about oncogenic mutations.

claim: The reporter splicing efficiency is >95% by qRT-PCR.
source: Reporter splicing efficiency >95% by qRT-PCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports a measurement of splicing efficiency from qRT-PCR.

claim: The cell line constitutively expresses PP7-mCherry and MS2-GFP under the control of a ubiquitin promoter.
source: The cell line also constitutively expresses the PP7 bacteriophage-coat protein fused to the mCherry fluorescent protein (PP7-mCherry) and the MS2 bacteriophage-coat proteins fused to the green fluorescent protein (MS2-GFP).
